questions.q: What does a branch policy on `main` typically enforce in Azure Repos?
options: That commits can never be reverted
A pull request, a minimum number of reviewers, and/or a passing pipeline run before a merge is allowed
That every repository must use the Classic pipeline designer
That all work items are automatically closed on push
questions.explain: Branch policies require things like a pull request, reviewer approval, and a passing pipeline run before the merge button unlocks — turning a pr trigger into an enforced gate.

questions.q: What happens when a commit message includes something like `Fixes #482`?
options: Nothing — work item references only work in pull request titles, not commit messages
Azure DevOps automatically links the commit to work item 482, connecting planning and shipping
The commit is automatically rejected by Azure Repos
Work item 482 is automatically deleted
questions.explain: Azure DevOps automatically links a commit or PR that references a work item ID, so anyone viewing that work item can trace the commit, PR, and eventual pipeline run that shipped it.

questions.q: What's the difference between a pipeline artifact and an Azure Artifacts feed?
options: They are the same thing with two different names
A pipeline artifact is build output scoped to one pipeline run; an Azure Artifacts feed is a longer-lived package registry shared across pipelines and developers
A pipeline artifact can only be a Docker image; an Artifacts feed can only hold npm packages
Azure Artifacts feeds are deprecated in favor of pipeline artifacts
questions.explain: A pipeline artifact, like the Docker@2 push in Lesson 12, is output passed within a single run. An Azure Artifacts feed is a persistent registry (npm, NuGet, Maven, universal) that any pipeline or developer can pull a published package from.

questions.q: Which Azure DevOps service holds work items organized into backlogs, sprints, and kanban boards?
options: Repos
Pipelines
Boards
Artifacts
questions.explain: Boards is the service dedicated to work item tracking — user stories, bugs, and tasks moving through a backlog, sprint, or kanban board.

questions.q: If Northbridge Retail wanted to publish a shared internal npm library that several services depend on, where should it live?
options: As a one-off pipeline artifact rebuilt by every consuming pipeline
In an Azure Artifacts feed, so any pipeline or developer can pull the published package
Directly inside the storefront-api repository's source code
As a variable group value
questions.explain: A shared, reusable library belongs in a longer-lived Azure Artifacts feed rather than being rebuilt as a short-lived pipeline artifact by every consumer.
